extracted.intended_audience: advanced_undergraduate or beginning graduate students in dynamical systems / applied mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying the mathematical criteria used to analyze the Poincaré map for the Lorenz model and related one-dimensional maps (g and logistic family), including definitions of chaos, orbit behavior, bifurcation criteria, and stability tests based on derivatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitive dependence on initial conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: A system/map has sensitive dependence if arbitrarily close initial points can have forward orbits that separate by an O(1) amount; specifically, given any point in the attractor (or any y0 ∈ I) and any neighborhood, one can find nearby seeds u0,v0 and n > 0 with |g^n(u0) − g^n(v0)| at least a prescribed positive amount (≥ 2ν in the text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved for g by showing g expands lengths by at least a fixed factor (>2) so some iterate sends a small interval across 0 and then near ±y*, producing large separations. Interpreted as the hallmark of chaotic behavior: tiny changes in initial position may cause drastic changes in eventual behavior. For interval maps the combination of transitivity and density of periodic points implies sensitive dependence (Banks et al.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Density of periodic points
rubrics_metrics.description: Periodic points (points y0 with g^n(y0)=y0 for some n>0) are dense in the interval I (and periodic points of the Poincaré map are dense in the attractor A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shown by mapping small subintervals one-to-one over (−y*,0) or (0,y*) under some iterate g^n so that g^n (or g^(n+1)) crosses the diagonal y=x on the subinterval, producing a periodic point inside any chosen subinterval. In terms of the flow, closed orbits are dense in A; many closed curves can be topologically knotted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: g is transitive on I if for any y1,y2 ∈ I and neighborhoods U1 of y1 and U2 of y2 there exists a point ˜y ∈ U1 and n > 0 such that g^n(˜y) ∈ U2. Equivalently (for interval maps) there exists an orbit dense in I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved using expansion in the y-direction and the ability to map subintervals to cover desired ranges; transitivity plus density of periodic points is used in the textbook to characterize chaos on the attractor. Existence of a dense orbit is often easier to check; the equivalence uses Baire Category Theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of chaos for interval maps
rubrics_metrics.description: A map f: I→I is called chaotic (textbook definition) if (1) periodic points are dense in I, (2) f is transitive on I, and (3) f has sensitive dependence on initial conditions (there exists β>0 such that arbitrarily close seeds eventually separate by >β).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For continuous maps of an interval the third condition is redundant (the first two imply it). Note there are multiple definitions in the literature (some use exponential separation, positive Lyapunov exponents, etc.); authors caution about these variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contraction in the x-direction (Poincaré map)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poincaré map (Φ) for the Lorenz model contracts distances in the x-direction by a uniform factor c<1; in particular, points on the same horizontal line are drawn closer in x under iteration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly in proofs: contraction in x ensures uniqueness of the limit point arising from nested images of horizontal intervals (so each backward orbit corresponds to a single point), allows estimates |Φ^k(x1,y) − Φ^k(x2,y)| ≤ c^k |x1−x2|, and is used to choose iterates so that images fit inside small target neighborhoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expansion in the y-direction for the reduced map g
rubrics_metrics.description: The one-dimensional map g (y↦g(y)) that describes the y-coordinate dynamics expands lengths (each iteration multiplies interval length by at least a fixed factor, stated as ≥ 2 in the text), with lim_{y→0±} g(y) = ∓y* and g odd: g(−y)=−g(y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expansion property is the mechanism producing sensitive dependence and the ability to map small intervals to cover large parts of I (used in proofs of density/transitivity). The graph of g has the indicated shape: two preimages for some points, one for others, endpoints ±y* have no preimages in I.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity of backward orbits and correspondence to attractor points
rubrics_metrics.description: Except for y0=±y*, any y0∈I has infinitely many distinct backward orbits (sequences ...,y−2,y−1,y0 with g(y−k)=y−k+1). Each such backward orbit corresponds to a unique point of the attractor A lying on the line {y=y0}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument uses that many points have two preimages and that nested images of horizontal lines under Φ produce a unique intersection point (uniqueness due to contraction in x). This gives the complicated (Cantor-like) transverse structure of A intersected with lines y=constant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attractor transverse structure: infinitely many intersections with horizontal lines
rubrics_metrics.description: The attractor A meets each line y=y0 (with |y0|<y*) in infinitely many distinct points. For forward time, through each of these points either the solution meets y=0 (hence tends to equilibrium at (0,0,0)) or continually reintersects R with successive intersection distances shrinking to 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This property follows from the backward-orbit multiplicity and contraction mechanism; it emphasizes that A is highly nontrivial and fractal-like across horizontal slices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed point / periodic point classification via derivative
rubrics_metrics.description: For a one-dimensional map f with fixed point x0: x0 is an attracting fixed point (sink) if |f'(x0)|<1, a repelling fixed point (source) if |f'(x0)|>1, and neutral/indifferent if |f'(x0)|=1 (cases |f'(x0)|=1 require further analysis). For periodic points, classify using derivative of f^n at the point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate consequence of the Mean Value Theorem: choose K with |f'|<K<1 on a neighborhood to get geometric contraction. Examples illustrate that derivative = 1 gives ambiguous behavior (examples f=x+x^3 source, g=x−x^3 sink, h=x+x^2 neither). If f'(x0)<0 nearby orbits alternate sides of x0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bifurcation criterion (derivative = +1 indicates a fixed-point bifurcation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fixed-point bifurcations (birth/death or change of stability of fixed points) in one-parameter families f_λ may occur only at parameter values where the derivative at the fixed point equals +1 (the Implicit Function Theorem argument identifies the generic saddle-node/tangent bifurcation at this condition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If f_λ0'(x0)=1 and f_λ0(x0)=x0, one cannot locally solve uniquely for fixed points without further terms; typical outcome is a saddle-node where a neutral fixed point splits into attracting and repelling branches as λ passes the bifurcation value. Exercises explore this further.

rubrics_metrics.name: Period-doubling bifurcation criterion (derivative = −1)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the derivative at a fixed (or periodic) point equals −1 at a parameter value, the fixed point may change stability and a period-doubling bifurcation (birth of an attracting 2-cycle) can occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example families illustrate the phenomenon: linear map λx at λ=−1 (all nonzero points lie on 2-cycles at λ=−1); quadratic family f_c(x)=x^2+c has period-doubling at c=−3/4 producing an attracting 2-cycle for nearby c-values. More complicated cascades occur for maps like the logistic map as parameter varies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logistic map stability and bifurcation thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: For f_λ(x)=λx(1−x) on I=[0,1]: 0 is a fixed point attracting for 0<λ≤1 and repelling for λ>1; a second fixed point x_λ=(λ−1)/λ exists for λ>1 and is attracting for 1<λ≤3 and repelling for λ>3; at λ=3 a period-doubling bifurcation occurs and more complex dynamics (period-doubling cascade and chaos) arise as λ increases toward 4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At λ=4 the map is topologically mixing: iterates f_4^n have 2^n fixed points, critical point behavior implies many subintervals are mapped onto the whole interval, and typical orbits appear chaotic; graphical iteration and numerical experiments illustrate this complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphical iteration as visualization and diagnostic tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Graphical iteration: plot y=f(x) and y=x; from (x_n,x_n) draw vertical to (x_n,f(x_n)) and horizontal to (x_{n+1},x_{n+1}) to visualize orbits, fixed points, and cycles and to judge attraction/repulsion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to see sinks, sources, cycles (e.g., 3-cycles), and to reason about bifurcations (saddle-node, period-doubling) and invariant sets. Also useful for checking whether orbits approach fixed points or cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preimage structure of g and implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Points in the interval [g(−y*), g(y*)] have two preimages under g, points in (−y*, g(−y*)) and (g(y*), y*) have only one, and endpoints ±y* have no preimages in I (g is undefined at 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This determines the branching structure of backward orbits (binary-like tree of preimages) and underlies the fractal transverse structure of the attractor and multiplicity of backward orbits per y0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model reduction principle: from flow to 1-D map
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the assumptions given, the 3D Lorenz flow can be reduced (via a Poincaré map) to a 2D map Φ on a rectangle R, and further (because Φ contracts in x and identifies dynamics by y) to a one-dimensional map g on I=[−y*,y*]; iteration of g determines the behavior of all solutions in the attractor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduction motivates studying expanding one-dimensional maps to understand complex 3D flows; proofs exploit contraction in x to ignore transverse coordinates and focus on y-iteration. Exercises and the subsequent chapter extend these ideas.
